name: Siddhāsana (the adept's seat)
method_summary: Seated with the heel of one foot pressing the perineum (yonisthāna) and the other foot placed above the genitals, body straight, chin on the chest (a form of jālandhara), senses restrained and the gaze fixed between the brows (HYP 1.35; GS 2.7; ŚS 3.85; GŚ 8). A second arrangement with the left ankle above the genitals is given 'by another view' (HYP 1.36). The texts call it the chief of postures, the one to sit in always.

names.name: vajrāsana / muktāsana / guptāsana (other names reported in HYP 1.37)

signs_of_progress: purifies the 72,000 channels (HYP 1.39)
with it kevala kumbhaka, unmanī and the three locks arise spontaneously (HYP 1.41-42)
practised with moderate diet and meditation on the self for twelve years it brings completion (HYP 1.40)
breaks open the door of liberation (HYP 1.35; GS 2.7)
duration: the HYP (1.40) speaks of twelve years of practice for completion

equivalents.note: HYP 1.37 reports that some call siddhāsana vajrāsana; GS 2.12 describes vajrāsana as a distinct posture.
HYP 1.37 reports the name muktāsana for it; GS 2.11 describes muktāsana separately.
HYP 1.37 reports the name guptāsana for it; GS 2.20 describes guptāsana separately.

notes: Brahmānanda (Jyotsnā on HYP 1.36) calls the first form Matsyendra's and the second that of another school. GŚ numbering per the GRETIL e-text (Kuvalayananda–Shukla).

name: Padmāsana (the lotus seat)
method_summary: Each foot placed on the opposite thigh. In the 'bound' form the hands cross behind the back to hold the big toes, the chin rests on the chest and the gaze is on the nose-tip (HYP 1.44; GS 2.8). In another form the soles are upturned on the thighs, the hands palms-up between the thighs, the gaze on the nose-tip, the tongue at the root of the front teeth and the breath drawn in slowly (HYP 1.45-47; DYŚ 31-35; ŚS 3.88-91). It is the seat for breath-practice in many texts (HYP 2.7, 2.59).
signs_of_progress: destroys all diseases (HYP 1.44, 1.47; DYŚ 35)
with prāṇa and apāna united in it, awakening through the power of śakti (HYP 1.48)
one who holds the breath in it is liberated (HYP 1.49)
notes: Listed in the Yoga-bhāṣya on YS 2.46. U10's paraphrase of that list omits vīrāsana; the unit recalls 'padmāsanaṃ vīrāsanaṃ bhadrāsanaṃ svastikaṃ …' — check the bhāṣya. Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Baddhapadmāsana (the bound lotus)
method_summary: Padmāsana with the arms crossed behind the back holding the big toes (HYP 1.44; GS 2.8); named as the seat for purifying the channels (HYP 2.7; GŚ 41, 43) and in Dattātreya's own posture (DYŚ 5).
notes: The Triśikhibrāhmaṇa lists baddhapadma separately from padma.

name: Siṃhāsana (the lion seat)
method_summary: The ankles placed under the scrotum at the sides of the perineum, crossed (left to the right side, right to the left), the hands on the knees with fingers spread, the mouth open, gazing at the nose-tip (HYP 1.50-52); in the Gheraṇḍa the knees rest on the ground and jālandhara is applied (GS 2.14-15).
signs_of_progress: brings about the three locks (HYP 1.52)
destroys all diseases (GS 2.15)
notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Bhadrāsana (the auspicious seat)
method_summary: The ankles under the scrotum at the sides of the perineum, the sides of the feet held firmly with the hands (HYP 1.53-54); in the Gheraṇḍa the ankles are crossed, the big toes held from behind, jālandhara applied and the gaze on the nose-tip (GS 2.9-10).
signs_of_progress: destroys all diseases (HYP 1.54; GS 2.10)

names.name: gorakṣāsana (so called by the siddha yogins, HYP 1.54)

equivalents.note: HYP 1.54 says the siddhas call bhadrāsana gorakṣāsana; GS 2.24-25 describes a distinct gorakṣāsana.

notes: Listed in the Yoga-bhāṣya on YS 2.46. U10's paraphrase of that list omits vīrāsana; the unit recalls 'padmāsanaṃ vīrāsanaṃ bhadrāsanaṃ svastikaṃ …' — check the bhāṣya.

name: Svastikāsana (the auspicious-mark seat)
method_summary: Both soles placed between the knees and thighs, sitting with the body straight (HYP 1.19; GS 2.13; ŚS 3.95). The Śivasaṃhitā calls it the comfortable posture (sukhāsana).
signs_of_progress: no disease enters the body and the breath is mastered (ŚS 3.96)

equivalents.note: ŚS 3.97 calls svastika sukhāsana; the Darśana and Triśikhibrāhmaṇa list sukha separately.

notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Gomukhāsana (the cow-face seat)
method_summary: The right ankle set beside the left buttock and the left beside the right, so that the legs resemble a cow's face (HYP 1.20); in the Gheraṇḍa the feet are on the ground with the heels by the sides of the back and the body steady (GS 2.16).
notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra. The Śivasaṃhitā (5.5) counts 'sitting in gomukha' among the obstacles that take the form of knowledge.

name: Vīrāsana (the hero's seat)
method_summary: One foot set firmly on the other thigh and the other thigh on the other foot (HYP 1.21); in the Gheraṇḍa one foot on the thigh and the other turned back (GS 2.17).
notes: Listed in the Yoga-bhāṣya on YS 2.46. U10's paraphrase of that list omits vīrāsana; the unit recalls 'padmāsanaṃ vīrāsanaṃ bhadrāsanaṃ svastikaṃ …' — check the bhāṣya. Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Muktāsana (the free seat)
method_summary: The left ankle at the root of the anus and the right ankle above it, with head, neck and body in line (GS 2.11); HYP 1.37 gives muktāsana as another name of siddhāsana; the Haṭhapradīpikā has the yogin sit in muktāsana to listen to the inner sound (HYP 4.67).
signs_of_progress: gives success (GS 2.11)
notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Vajrāsana (the thunderbolt seat)
method_summary: The thighs made firm like a thunderbolt and the feet placed by the sides of the anus (GS 2.12); it is the seat for khecarī in the Śivasaṃhitā (4.31) and for śakticālana in the Haṭhapradīpikā (3.114-115). HYP 1.37 records vajrāsana as another name for siddhāsana.
signs_of_progress: gives success to yogins (GS 2.12)

name: Guptāsana (the hidden seat)
method_summary: The feet hidden between the knees and thighs and the anus placed on the feet (GS 2.20); HYP 1.37 gives guptāsana as another name of siddhāsana.

name: Sukhāsana (the comfortable seat)
method_summary: A comfortable seated posture: in the Śivasaṃhitā the name is given to svastika (ŚS 3.97); the Gheraṇḍa has sagarbha breath-control done 'seated in sukhāsana' (GS 5.49); the Darśana and Triśikhibrāhmaṇa Upaniṣads list sukha among their postures.

name: Yogāsana (the yoga seat)
method_summary: The feet, turned up, placed on the knees and the hands, turned up, on the seat, drawing in the breath and gazing at the nose-tip — a posture for yoga-practice (GS 2.44-45); also listed in the Triśikhibrāhmaṇa.

name: Gorakṣāsana (Gorakṣa's seat)
method_summary: The feet turned up between the knees and thighs, the heels covered with the upturned hands, the throat contracted and the gaze on the nose-tip (GS 2.24-25). In HYP 1.54 'gorakṣāsana' is the siddhas' name for bhadrāsana.
signs_of_progress: a cause of success for yogins (GS 2.25)

name: Kūrmāsana (the tortoise seat)
method_summary: The anus closed firmly with the ankles placed in reverse order (HYP 1.22); in the Gheraṇḍa the ankles crossed under the scrotum with body, head and neck straight (GS 2.32).

name: Matsyendrāsana (Matsyendra's seat)
method_summary: A seated twist: one foot at the root of the opposite thigh and the other wound outside the knee, the body turned and the feet held (HYP 1.26); in the Gheraṇḍa the left foot is placed on the right knee, the right elbow set on it, the face resting on the right hand and the gaze between the brows (GS 2.22-23).
signs_of_progress: kindles the digestive fire, destroys terrible diseases, awakens kuṇḍalinī and steadies the moon (HYP 1.27)

name: Paścimatānāsana (the stretch of the back; paścimottāna, ugrāsana)
method_summary: The legs stretched on the ground like a staff, the tips of the feet held with the hands and the forehead brought to the knees (HYP 1.28; GS 2.26). The Śivasaṃhitā's 'fierce posture' (ugrāsana), with the legs apart and the head on the knees, is expressly identified with paścimottāna (ŚS 3.92). It is also the base for dry basti and taḍāgī mudrā (GS 1.48, 3.61).
signs_of_progress: makes the breath flow in the back (central) channel, kindles the digestive fire, slims the belly, gives health (HYP 1.29)
kindles the breath and removes bodily decline (ŚS 3.92)

name: Utkaṭāsana (the squat on the toes)
method_summary: The ground supported by the toes, the heels raised, the anus set upon the heels (GS 2.27). It is the posture taken in water for basti (HYP 2.26; GS 1.46).

name: Saṅkaṭāsana (the constricted seat)
method_summary: The left leg set on the ground and the right leg wound around the left, with the hands on the knees (GS 2.28).
notes: The e-text wording is terse; details of the leg placement are uncertain.

name: Vṛṣāsana (the bull seat)
method_summary: The anus set on the right ankle and the other foot, turned the other way, on the left side touching the ground (GS 2.38).

name: Garuḍāsana (the Garuḍa seat)
method_summary: Pressing the ground with shins and thighs, the body steadied by the knees, the hands on the knees (GS 2.37).
notes: The Gheraṇḍa's garuḍāsana is not the modern standing posture of the same name.

name: Maṇḍūkāsana (the frog)
method_summary: The soles turned back, the big toes touching and the knees set forward (GS 2.34).

name: Uttānamaṇḍūkāsana (the supine frog)
method_summary: From the frog posture, holding the head with the elbows and lying back like a frog (GS 2.35).

name: Matsyāsana (the fish)
method_summary: In the lotus with the feet free (muktapadmāsana), lying supine and encircling the head with the elbows (GS 2.21); also listed in the Triśikhibrāhmaṇa.
signs_of_progress: destroys disease (GS 2.21)

name: Kukkuṭāsana (the cockerel)
method_summary: From padmāsana the hands are inserted between the knees and thighs, planted on the ground, and the body raised into the air (HYP 1.23; GS 2.31).

name: Uttānakūrmāsana (the supine tortoise)
method_summary: From the bound kukkuṭa position the neck is clasped with the arms and one lies back like a tortoise on its back (HYP 1.24; GS 2.33).

name: Mayūrāsana (the peacock)
method_summary: The palms pressed to the ground, the sides of the navel resting on the elbows, the body raised horizontal in the air like a staff (HYP 1.30; GS 2.29).
signs_of_progress: quickly removes gulma, abdominal swellings and other diseases; overcomes the doṣas; 'burns up' bad food; kindles the digestive fire; digests even the poison kālakūṭa (HYP 1.31; GS 2.30)
notes: Yoga Yājñavalkya ch. 3 is recalled (low confidence) to describe eight postures: svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra.

name: Dhanurāsana (the bow)
method_summary: In the Haṭhapradīpikā the big toes are held with the hands and drawn up to the ear like a drawn bow (HYP 1.25); in the Gheraṇḍa the legs are stretched on the ground, the feet held from behind and the body curved like a bow (GS 2.18).
notes: The two texts describe different forms under one name.

name: Śavāsana (the corpse; mṛtāsana)
method_summary: Lying supine on the ground like a corpse (HYP 1.32; GS 2.19); the Dattātreyayogaśāstra counts lying like a corpse, relaxed in solitude, among the 'signals' of laya-yoga (DYŚ 22-23).
signs_of_progress: removes fatigue and brings rest to the mind (HYP 1.32; GS 2.19)
notes: Later 'yoga-nidrā' teachings built on this posture belong to recent lineages (U52).

name: Śalabhāsana (the locust)
method_summary: Lying face down with the hands (palms) on the ground by the chest, the feet raised a span into the air (GS 2.39).

name: Makarāsana (the crocodile)
method_summary: Lying face down with the chest on the ground and the legs stretched out, the head held with the arms (GS 2.40).
signs_of_progress: increases the bodily fire (GS 2.40)

name: Uṣṭrāsana (the camel)
method_summary: Lying face down, the feet turned up behind and held with the hands, the mouth and belly firmly contracted (GS 2.41).
notes: The Gheraṇḍa's form is prone, unlike the modern kneeling posture of this name.

name: Bhujaṅgāsana (the serpent)
method_summary: From the toes to the navel the body rests on the ground; supporting the ground with the palms one raises the head like a serpent (GS 2.42-43).
signs_of_progress: the bodily fire increases, all diseases are destroyed and the serpent goddess (kuṇḍalinī) awakens (GS 2.43)

name: Vṛkṣāsana (the tree)
method_summary: Standing on the left leg with the right foot set at the root of the left thigh, like a tree (GS 2.36).

name: Daṇḍāsana (the staff seat)
method_summary: Named among the examples of posture in Vyāsa's bhāṣya on YS 2.46 ('posture is steady and comfortable'). The bhāṣya gives only the name; its form is explained by the commentators (Vācaspati Miśra, Vijñānabhikṣu and others), whose descriptions are not reproduced here.
notes: Name certain; form per commentators not recalled with confidence.

name: The postures of the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati (group entry)
method_summary: A prose haṭha manual that describes more than a hundred postures (about 112 are counted), set in a sequence after the yamas, niyamas and cleansing acts and before breath-control and mudrā; many are dynamic or repeated movements and some use a rope. Its postures reappear, illustrated, in the Mysore Śrītattvanidhi. The individual names are not recalled with enough confidence to be entered here (see REPORT).
notes: Group entry standing in for the individual postures the unit could not responsibly name.

name: The eighty-four postures of the Jogapradīpikā (group entry)
method_summary: The Brajbhāṣā Jogapradīpikā (18th c.) teaches eighty-four postures, alongside mudrās and other practices; the individual names are not recalled with enough confidence to be entered here.

name: The eighty-four postures of the Haṭharatnāvalī (group entry)
method_summary: The Haṭharatnāvalī (ch. 3) names eighty-four postures and describes a selection, repeating the Haṭhapradīpikā's descriptions for several (siddha, padma, siṃha, bhadra and others) and adding many variants; the full list is not entered here because the unit could not recall it reliably (see REPORT for candidate names to check).
